issues.legal_issue: The High Court’s rent-control revisional jurisdiction permits review of the factual correctness of the trial court’s order but does not extend to a full rehearing as on first appeal.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the trial court’s eviction order in revision.
The High Court considered a commissioner’s report and sketch, which both parties relied on, and reassessed the accommodation available to the landlord.
The High Court reversed the trial court’s decision after finding that the landlord’s accommodation was sufficient.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to examine whether the trial court’s factual findings were correct in light of the evidence, while its revisional power remained narrower than first-appellate jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 50(1) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 empowers the High Court to examine the legality or correctness of the order or proceeding. Central Tobacco Co. v. Chandra Prakash and Bhoolchand v. Kay Pee Cee Investments establish that this permits correction of factual as well as legal errors, but does not make revision equivalent to an appeal, particularly where findings depend on the credibility of witnesses. Dattopant Gopalvarao Devakate v. Vithalrao Maruthirao Janagaval likewise recognizes that the revisional power is wider than the power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure but is not a second first appeal.

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding before the High Court was a revision from a trial court’s order in a rent-control dispute.
predicates.correctness_review_authorized: The applicable review standard required the High Court to examine whether the challenged order was factually correct as well as lawful.

issues.definition: When a rent-control dispute reaches the High Court in revision under a standard requiring review of correctness, the High Court may examine factual correctness but may not treat the proceeding as a full first appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord is not entitled to eviction for personal occupation when the available accommodation is sufficient to meet the reasonable needs of the landlord’s household.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession of the tenant’s part of the ground floor, asserting that the accommodation available to his family was insufficient.
The landlord already occupied a substantial part of the ground floor and the whole first floor of the building.

A commissioner’s report and sketch showed the rooms available to the landlord, and the court found that those rooms could accommodate the landlord, his wife, children, and widowed mother, as well as their dining, kitchen, study, and guest needs.
The Supreme Court accepted that the landlord’s desire for additional space was bona fide but held that the existing accommodation met the household’s needs.
issues.conclusion: The landlord had not established the reasonable and bona fide requirement necessary for an eviction decree; the High Court’s dismissal of the suit was sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(h) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 requires the landlord’s need to be both bona fide and reasonable. The landlord is ordinarily the best judge of residential needs, as recognized in Meenal Eknath Kshirsagar v. Traders & Agencies and Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan, but the court must assess whether the existing accommodation is sufficient in light of the household’s needs. Those cases did not assist a landlord already occupying substantial accommodation where the evidence showed no genuine need for additional space.

predicates.requirement_based_eviction_case: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the premises were required for the landlord’s own or household’s occupation.
predicates.substantial_existing_accommodation: The landlord already occupied a substantial amount of accommodation in the same building.
predicates.existing_space_meets_household_needs: The available accommodation could meet the reasonable residential needs of the landlord’s household.

issues.definition: If a landlord seeks eviction for household occupation while already occupying substantial accommodation that meets the household’s reasonable needs, the landlord is not entitled to eviction on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may grant an occupant additional time to vacate when the occupant agrees to do so even if the occupant succeeds in the appeal.
material_facts: The tenant informed the Court that he would vacate after a period of time and his counsel confirmed that the tenant would abide by that position even if the tenant succeeded in the proceedings.
The Court confirmed that the tenant must provide a written undertaking to vacate and continue paying the agreed amounts until vacating.
issues.conclusion: The Court used its constitutional power to direct the tenant to vacate by the time agreed to, subject to filing the required undertaking and continuing payments.
issues.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Constitution of India empowers the Supreme Court to make an order to do complete justice in a matter before it. The Court exercised that power in light of the tenant’s confirmed agreement to vacate even if successful, and made the direction subject to a written undertaking and continued payments.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_in_eviction_case: The Supreme Court was deciding an appeal arising from an eviction dispute.
predicates.occupant_agreed_to_vacate_after_addition: The occupant agreed to leave the premises after being allowed additional time.
predicates.occupant_agreed_to_vacate_even_if_succes: The occupant’s counsel confirmed that the occupant would honor the agreement even if the occupant succeeded in the appeal.

issues.definition: When an occupant in an eviction appeal agrees to leave after additional time even if successful, the Supreme Court may grant that time subject to an undertaking.
